O.outcome_detail: difficulties with isolated components and covering all content

cells.quote: Survey data from teachers across five years of implementation (Faddis et al., 2011) indicated overall satisfaction with the curriculum and preparation, though some teachers, particularly those new to the program, had difficulties with isolated components and covering all content.
cells.note: No study text is available; quote copied from the wiki entry. The entry does not report inferential significance or an effect size for this comparison.

cells.quote: Buy-in and satisfaction tended to be more positive for middle school teachers than for high school teachers.

cells.quote: Bootstrapped independent-samples t tests showed that, on average, parents in the XtraMath group reported higher general feasibility of the training compared with the Cogmed group (see Table 2), representing a medium-sized effect, d = 0.56.
cells.note: The intervention lasted 5 weeks with training 5 times per week; the feasibility questionnaire was completed at the post-intervention assessment.

O.outcome_detail: teacher-rated academic performance growth at 12-month follow-up

cells.quote: Bootstrapped linear regressions showed that academic growth to post test was significantly higher in the math intervention group (B = 0.25 [95% confidence interval: 0.04–0.50], p = 0.039), but this difference was not sustained at the 12-month follow-up (B = 0.00 [−0.31 to 0.34], p = 0.996).
cells.note: The 12-month comparison was the hierarchically ordered second hypothesis. The study reported power for detecting relatively large effects, but no equivalence test; therefore the nonsignificant result is coded ns rather than 0.

O.outcome_detail: DEMAT standardized math test score growth at post test

cells.quote: There were no relevant group differences in math test score growth according to training condition (baseline DEMAT entered as covariate) post test: B = 0.05 [−0.20 to 0.29], p = 0.697; 12-month follow-up: B = 0.16 [−0.13 to 0.49], p = 0.346); however, inspection of Fig. 3 suggests that children in the XtraMath group achieved stable performance, while children in the active control group (Cogmed), on average, showed a tendency for decreasing math test performance after participating in the training.
cells.note: Secondary outcome: DEMAT 1+ was administered at baseline and post test.

O.outcome_detail: DEMAT standardized math test score growth at 12-month follow-up

cells.quote: There were no relevant group differences in math test score growth according to training condition (baseline DEMAT entered as covariate) post test: B = 0.05 [−0.20 to 0.29], p = 0.697; 12-month follow-up: B = 0.16 [−0.13 to 0.49], p = 0.346); however, inspection of Fig. 3 suggests that children in the XtraMath group achieved stable performance, while children in the active control group (Cogmed), on average, showed a tendency for decreasing math test performance after participating in the training.
cells.note: Secondary outcome: DEMAT 2+ was administered at the 12-month follow-up.

O.outcome_detail: completed training sessions per week during the 5-week intervention

cells.quote: With regard to training compliance across the 5-week intervention period, log-files showed that, on average, children in the XtraMath group completed fewer sessions per week (4.41 (0.98)) than children in the Cogmed group (5.11 (0.47) mean difference: 0.70 [95% CI: 0.28–1.12], p = 0.002).
cells.note: The reported mean difference is presented as a positive value despite XtraMath having fewer sessions; it appears to represent Cogmed minus XtraMath.
